rows.why: S1 expects a code that repeats an existing one to be drawn again. Item 7 asks what happens on a collision, and its pick redraws. The 14-day expiry part is basic setup; item 2 is about the boundary instant, which is S4.
S2 is the basic redeem path: access to that task only, and usedBy plus usedAt recorded. No item leaves this open. Item 10 is about checking the contributor ID, which S2 does not test.
Item 5 asks how a typed code is matched. Its pick strips whitespace and '-' and uppercases, so lowercase, spaced and hyphenated input all give the same code.
Item 2 asks whether the code is still valid at exactly 14 days. Its pick treats now >= expiresAt as expired, so it can be redeemed at 08:59:59.999 and fails with 'expired' at 09:00:00.

The open part of S5 is c1 redeeming their own used code again, a case where the code is used and the contributor already has access. Item 4 asks which check wins there. Its pick checks code state first, so c1 gets 'used', but S5 expects success with no change. (c2 getting 'used' is basic behaviour.)

Item 8 asks about revoking, including revoking a used code. Its pick adds revocation and throws for used codes, so a used code cannot be revoked. Unknown and revoked codes failing on redeem follows from its states.

Item 3 asks what happens when a contributor redeems a code for a task they already have access to. Its pick refuses with 'already has access' and leaves the code unused, which is exactly what S7 expects.
Item 11 asks how overlapping operations are handled. Its pick runs everything through a single promise queue, so one redeem wins and the other sees 'used', even when store calls resolve late.

The open part of S9 is that a used code stays 'used' after its expiry time. Item 1 asks how overlapping states are ranked, and its pick puts used first, so it stays 'used'. Item 12 (order) is about list order, which S9 does not test.
